name: Clothing brand
blurb: Design your own clothing, get it produced in small runs and sell it under your brand
title: How to Start a Clothing Brand: Costs, Steps and Risks
description: How to start a clothing brand: how it makes money, production and labelling basics, who it suits, stock and IP risks, and how to pre-sell a first drop cheaply.
h1: How to start a clothing brand
answer: Starting a clothing brand means designing garments, having them made by a manufacturer or decorating blank garments, and selling them under your own name, usually online first. You earn the gap between the retail price and production, shipping, marketing and returns. The catch is that factories often require minimum orders, unsold sizes become dead stock, and the brand only works if you can build an audience that cares about it.

sections.h: How a clothing brand makes money
body: Most small brands sell direct to customers through their own online store, social media and pop-up markets, sometimes adding wholesale to boutiques later at a lower price per piece.

Profit per item is the retail price minus fabric and production, samples, labels and packaging, shipping, payment fees, marketing and returns. Leftover sizes and colours that do not sell are the big hidden cost, which is why many brands sell in small "drops" and pre-orders.

ul: A clear point of view: who the clothes are for and why they would choose you.
Designs and tech packs (measurements, materials, construction) a manufacturer can follow, or quality blank garments to decorate.
A manufacturer or decorator, found through samples rather than promises, and money for a first small run.

Labels that meet local rules. In the US, the FTC's textile rules require fibre content, country of origin and the maker's or seller's identity on most garments, plus permanent care instructions; other countries have their own labelling laws.
An online store, product photos and a plan for reaching your first buyers.
Business registration, tax setup and a trademark search on your brand name; check local rules.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People with a real community or style niche to design for
Anyone who just wants a logo on generic T-shirts
Creators comfortable promoting themselves on social media
People without savings for samples and a first run
Patient builders who can live with slow early sales
Anyone expecting the product alone to sell itself

ul: Dead stock: guessing sizes and quantities wrong ties up cash; start small and pre-sell.
Manufacturing problems: quality that differs from samples, delays and hidden costs. Get prices and specifications in writing.
Trademark and copyright: a brand name already registered by someone else, or designs that copy logos or artwork, can force a rebrand or bring claims.
Saturation: many new brands look alike; without a distinct audience, marketing costs rise.
"Brand launch" agencies and courses that charge heavily upfront while promising quick success.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Describe your customer in one sentence and find where they spend time online and offline.
Mock up three designs and ask that audience which they would buy, and at what price.
Make a small batch on blanks or through print-on-demand to check the response before a factory order.
Open pre-orders for one piece with an honest delivery date.
Cost the full production run per unit, including samples, labels and shipping, before committing.
Search trademark registers for your brand name, then register the business.
Order samples from two or three manufacturers and compare quality and terms.
Plan one small drop with limited sizes and colours.
Set up a simple store and start posting the making-of process to build an audience.
Track sell-through by size and colour to plan the next run.

faq.q: How much money do I need to start a clothing brand?
faq.a: It depends on whether you decorate blanks, use print-on-demand or work with a factory that sets minimum order quantities. Get quotes for samples and a first run from real manufacturers before deciding; that is the cost that matters.

faq.q: Do I need to trademark my clothing brand name?
faq.a: It is wise to at least search existing registrations before launching, and many brands register their name once it gains traction. Rules and costs differ by country, so check your national trademark office.

faq.q: Should I start with print on demand?
faq.a: It is a low-risk way to test designs and audience, but margins are thin and quality control is limited. Many brands move to small production runs once they know what sells.
